Adani rival GMR plans $2 billion expansion at two India airports

The plans come as demand is surging in the world’s third-largest domestic aviation market, trailing only the US and China.

Mihir Mishra

24 August, 2026 12:40 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Travelers at Indira Gandhi International Airport in New Delhi, India, on Aug. 24, 2021. | T. Narayan/Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

GMR Airports Ltd., the main competitor to Adani Group’s airports operator, is planning to spend as much as 194 billion rupees ($2 billion) to expand its New Delhi and Hyderabad facilities, a sign of bullish expectations for India’s aviation market over the coming decade.

The investments, spread over the next five to seven years, are aimed at boosting capacity and modernizing infrastructure to keep pace with rapidly rising passenger volumes, Saurabh Chawla, company’s executive director for finance and strategy said in an interview.

The plans come as demand is surging in the world’s third-largest domestic aviation market, trailing only the US and China. India’s flier traffic is projected to grow six-fold to around 1.1 billion passengers over the next 14 years, while its commercial airline fleet is seen increasing from 400 planes as of 2014 to more than   2,350 aircraft by 2040, according to government estimates. The company is earmarking about 138 billion rupees for Rajiv Gandhi International Airport in the southern industrial hub of Hyderabad and as much as 56 billion rupees for the New Delhi airport, Chawla said. The investments will be funded by a mix of debt and equity by the respective airport ventures and not directly tied to GMR Airports, which is the holding company.

Show Full Article

Once completed, Hyderabad’s upgraded airport will be able to accommodate about 80 million passengers, or more than double its current annual volume of 34 million fliers.

GMR Airports is India’s largest airport operator by number of fliers annually while rival Adani Airport Holdings Ltd. is the biggest by number of airports. The Adani conglomerate is looking to invest $15 billion to boost passenger capacity at its aviation facilities over the next five years, Bloomberg News reported in December.

Build-Outs Chawla said the build-outs in New Delhi and Hyderabad may be just the beginning of a modernization drive at GMR Airports, whose portfolio includes six airports in India, one in the Philippines and another under construction in Greece.

“Investment plans for the new airport at Nagpur, just taken over in June 2026, are under discussions,” he said.

GMR Airports, in which France’s Aeroports de Paris SA owns 26.5%, will focus on bidding for local airport projects that the Indian government plans to sell, Chawla said, adding that no discussions are underway involving redevelopment of overseas airport projects.

The senior executive also said the Hyderabad-based GMR Group isn’t keen to enter the airline business, even if the Indian government tweaks the rules to permit such a move.

India is discussing a policy change that would allow airport operators to run airlines, Bloomberg reported last month. The government wants to boost competition given that two airlines — IndiGo and Air India — control nearly 90% of the local market.

“We’re not interested,” Chawla said, explaining the group wants to stay focused on its core airport business and related operations such as aircraft maintenance and real estate development around its aviation facilities.

3 things that are wrong with BJP’s Vande Mataram politics

In Modi-Shah’s rejection of the two-stanza version also lies the suggestion that they are bigger nationalists and patriots than Gandhi, Tagore, Bose, Patel and Nehru.

D.K. Singh

24 August, 2026 11:46 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File photo of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah | Photo: T. Narayan | Bloomberg

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

T he BJP has put the Congress on the spot over nationalism again. Or so goes the chatter in political circles. See how the principal opposition party has dug itself into a hole over Vande Mataram, our national song.

Kerala Chief Minister VD Satheesan did away with the national song at the official flag-hoisting ceremony on Independence Day. His counterparts—DK Shiv a kumar, Revanth Reddy and Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu—in three other Congress-ruled states chose to comply with Amit Shah-led Home Ministry’s order to sing all six stanzas of Vande Mataram.

At the Congress headquarters in New Delhi, as the singing went beyond the second stanza, there were red faces all around. Sonia Gandhi, Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge were visibly dismayed. And, no, Sonia wasn’t asking for a chair for Kharge. Everybody saw what was happening. The Congress was at sixes and sevens about the six-stanza national song. The Gandhis should sack the general secretary (organisation), KC Venugopal, for making a joke of the party on such a sensitive issue.

Show Full Article

The BJP loved it. When it comes to issues related to nationalism or religion, trust the Congress to dig a hole for itself. And here was a blend of both. When the Congress Working Committee (CWC) later decided to stick to the original two-stanza Vande Mataram, the BJP doubled down. It accused the Opposition party of minority appeasement because there are references to Hindu goddesses—Durga, Kamala (Lakshmi) and Vanee (Saraswati)—in the fifth stanza.

On Saturday, when newly appointed office-bearers met at the BJP headquarters, cameras were in place for the six-stanza national song. Most of the leaders were just lip-syncing. Questioning others’ nationalism is easier; memorising six stanzas requires true belief and commitment. I would also lip-sync if I were asked to sing all six stanzas without a teleprompter or a written text.

Having said that, the government and the BJP expending all their time and energy on Vande Mataram shows they have learnt the wrong lessons from the drubbing they got from ‘cockroaches’: that they need to double down on performative nationalism and communal binary in their politics. This approach is problematic on at least three counts.

A disconnect with India First, it suggests their refusal to see the headwinds. As I was writing it on Sunday , I glanced at the headlines in the last two days’ newspapers strewn on the table. “Rashtrapati Bhawan announces, retracts Rahman visit statement,” read one headline. Basically, the President’s office virtually declared Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to India, only to withdraw it an hour later.

As we were discussing this flip-flop the previous evening in our newsroom, a colleague quipped, “basically, the left arm didn’t know what the right arm was doing”. This used to happen during the Manmohan Singh government, especially in its second term. When did this start happening in the Modi government? The Rashtrapati Bha v an blooper only drew attention to the fact that Dhaka was keeping New Delhi on tenterhooks. We invite their PM, and this is how they respond! Our Vishwaguru edifice can’t be crumbling like this!

I reached out for a Hindi paper. It had a screaming headline on the front page: “Skyrocketing sugar price before festivals: selling at Rs. 70 per kg, an increase of Rs.17 in one month.” I reached out to another Hindi paper to find another screaming headline: “Rahul sat on dharna at the police station for seven hours, only then FIR of youth injured with 200 pellets registered.”

So, a common man needs the opposition leader’s help to lodge an FIR even in the national capital. Think of the message it sent. Front pages could be a bit loud, I thought. I decided to flip through inside pages. On top of the business page was another headline: “Inflation reaches from travel to kitchen: rice, biscuit, car, tyre, paint costlier by 18 per cent.” Another front page headline was: “Reality of recruitments in the Central government: vacancies in the last one decade go from 4.2 lakhs to 8.24 lakhs.”

Where does the Vande Mataram headline fit on these pages? There appears to be a disconnect between what’s happening in ordinary people’s lives and how those in power view them. Do those running the government and the BJP really believe that four extra stanzas can answer all the questions people may have about 12 years of governance?

It would be delulu politics in Gen Z parlance. If those running the show know this, why are they so stuck on the national song issue, instead of trying to focus their energy on governance and address issues that are bringing the people to the streets for protest? There can be only two reasons—confidence or helplessness. Confident because they know how to win elections, and that’s the only thing that matters. Jo jita wahi Sikandar . Or helpless because they don’t know any other way.

The second problem with the BJP’s Vande Mataram politics is an implied suggestion that PM Modi and HM Shah are better than Mahatma Gandhi, Subhas Chandra Bose, Rabindranath Tagore, Jawaharlal Nehru and Sardar Patel put together. The freedom fighters, Nobel laureates, and composer of our national anthem had held extensive deliberations before they decided to go with only two stanzas of Vande Mataram as India’s national song. It was Sardar Patel who seconded the resolution on the two-stanza song at the 1937 CWC meeting.

In Modi-Shah’s rejection of the two-stanza version also lies the suggestion that they are bigger nationalists and patriots than Gandhi, Tagore, Bose, Patel and Nehru. It’s a flattering thought, for sure. Look at the level of confidence. The Constituent Assembly had adopted the two-stanza Vande Mataram as our national song. It has been changed to six stanzas simply by a Home Ministry order signed by a joint secretary. It amounts to belittling our Constitution-makers.

Also read: Indian politicians need to learn to take a joke

The Viksit Bharat question The third problem with the BJP’s Vande Mataram politics is that it seems to be driven by immediate political objectives, not long-term interests of the country. Modi sang the same two-stanza song on every Independence Day for 24 years—first as Gujarat CM and then the Prime Minister—happily. What suddenly happened in the 26th year?

The bigger question is whether a government that promises to make India a developed country by 2047 can afford to embark on a polarising mission. Let me cite just one instance. The Home Ministry’s February order also said, “In all schools, the day’s work may begin with community singing of the National Song. School authorities should make adequate provision in their programmes for popularising the singing of the National Song….”

On the face of it, it sounds like an innocuous suggestion. Think of a zealous BJP CM making the singing of a six-stanza national song mandatory in “all schools”—government, private, mad ra sas, missionary schools, et al. It can potentially create trouble in every village, kasba and town.

There goes the dream of a Viksit Bharat.

DK Singh is Political Editor at ThePrint. He tweets @dksingh73. Views are personal.

(Edited by Saptak Datta)

Indian food safety officer shakes up Mumbai, one viral raid at a time

Reuters

24 August, 2026 08:30 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Arpan Chaturvedi, Vibhuti Sharma and Dhwani Pandya MUMBAI, Aug 24 (Reuters) – Tukaram Mundhe is an Indian bureaucrat on a mission.

As a state food safety commissioner, the 51-year-old has raided food businesses in the country’s commercial capital Mumbai in an unprecedented crackdown on poor hygiene and unsafe food that has captivated the public nationwide.

Mundhe has led the suspension of food permits of four Domino’s and one Pizza Hut outlet in recent weeks, and has also targeted cricket clubs, hotels and well-known restaurants in over 3,000 raids since he took over as Maharashtra’s food safety chief in May.

Show Full Article

When a Mumbai judge accused Mundhe of selective aggression towards private outlets and asked if court canteens were checked, his teams conducted inspections there within hours, shutting some of them which operated without licenses.

“Those who try to not comply, they will face what is expected from the regulator,” Mundhe said in an interview with Reuters, talking about his no-nonsense approach.

“You are dealing with the lives of people.”

Mundhe has won widespread public admiration across India because he has tapped into deep public frustration. Even though foreign chains such as Domino’s and McDonald’s are fast expanding, it is local eateries, roadside kiosks and small restaurants — long dogged by concerns over hygiene — that remain hugely popular.

Each year since 2020, Indian food inspectors have checked more than 100,000 food samples and found roughly 20% to be unsafe, substandard or lacking proper labels, government data shows. Nearly 8,000 food business licenses have been cancelled in the last three years.

“Everyone has tried to normalise this for years by saying it happens in India. It’s basically bottled-up anger,” said Ankur Bisen, a partner at consumer consulting firm The Knowledge Company.

“I have never seen anyone like Mundhe. It’s giving people hope.”

FINDING RATS AND EXPIRED FOOD

Mundhe, who is bespectacled and sports a chevron moustache, has an unconventional operating style.

He has featured in TV interviews declaring nobody dare bribe him, and that he is not afraid of administrative action despite being transferred numerous times in his 21-year career as an officer of the highly regarded Indian Administrative Service. “I get transferred every year,” he said in a 2018 interview.

Now, his food safety team’s actions go viral daily — raids lead to detailed public statements and graphic images that show interiors of eateries and grocery warehouses with stained walls, crawling cockroaches and rats, and even expired food — photos that have shocked many Indians.

“It was surprising. I did not expect these many violations,” Mundhe said.

In Mumbai, Reuters visits last week to 25 street vendors and restaurants showed heightened fear about Mundhe’s raids. One vendor has swapped artificial red dye for natural chilli in Chinese offerings, while another has started changing his frying oil three times a day and requires staff to wear gloves and head caps.

Mumbai’s omnipresent street food ‘vada pav’ — a spicy potato patty in a bun — has not escaped Mundhe’s attention. In June, he prohibited use of newspapers as packaging material — often used to wrap the delicacy.

Customers are noticing the change and consuming street food more confidently. Supriya Wagle, 14, is happy her favourite vada pav is now being packed in cleaner butter paper, saying that is “surely a relief”.

CRITICISM AMID CELEBRITY STATUS

After finding lapses at some Domino’s and Pizza Hut stores, Mundhe’s team on Friday suspended the permit of a McDonald’s outlet after finding “live pest activity (cockroaches)” and “rotting food”. The three companies did not respond to Reuters queries.

Mundhe’s crackdown has included action against a Mumbai British-era cricket club, a 70-year-old ice cream parlour and a 110-year-old Parsi Dairy.

He is facing criticism from businesses that say they should be given time to adapt, with some approaching the High Court and accusing his department of high-handedness.

In one case, the judges fined his department 500,000 rupees ($5,225) for continued suspension of an eatery even though it improved its compliance.

“If there are observations by the court, we take it seriously … if there is scope for improvement, we improve,” Mundhe said.

At an event in New Delhi on Friday, fans clicked quick selfies with Mundhe and jostled to shake his hand. One fan told him Prime Minister Narendra Modi should give him a national role.

“I don’t think I’m a celebrity. I’m just a food safety commissioner,” he told Reuters.

(Editing by Aditya Kalra and Muralikumar Anantharaman)
